title: Monolith vs Microservices
description: Compare monolithic and microservices architectures across deployment, scaling, and team structure.

data.text: A **monolithic architecture** packages an entire application as a single deployable unit. A **microservices architecture** splits the application into small, independently deployable services that communicate over the network. This lesson compares both styles across deployment, scaling, team structure, and operational complexity.

terms.definition: A single deployable unit containing all application code and logic.
A small, independently deployable service that owns a specific business capability.
A single entry point that routes requests to the appropriate microservice.
The logical separation between two services based on business capability.

data.text: Monolithic applications are built as one unit, while microservices are built as many small services. Each approach has distinct trade-offs in deployment, scaling, and team organization.

items: Monolith: Deploy once as a single artifact (WAR, JAR, EXE, container)
Microservices: Deploy each service independently with its own CI/CD pipeline
Monolith: Rolling updates require full restart
Microservices: Blue-green and canary deployments per service

data.text: Monolithic teams organize around technical layers (frontend, backend, database). Microservices teams organize around business capabilities, with each team owning one or more services end to end. This aligns with Conway's Law: system design tends to mirror the communication structure of the organization.

**Netflix** migrated from a monolithic DVD-rental application to hundreds of microservices to handle 200M+ subscribers. **Amazon** decomposed its retail monolith into services like catalog, cart, and checkout. **Uber** split its ride-matching, pricing, and payments into separate services to support rapid geographic expansion.

cards.title: Monolith
pros: Easy to test end to end

data.caption: Monolith vs Microservices Architecture
data.definition:
flowchart TD
    subgraph Monolith[🏢 Monolithic Architecture]
        M1[Single Codebase] --> M2[Single Build] --> M3[Single Deployment] --> M4[Single Runtime Process] --> M5[(Shared Database)]
    end
    subgraph Microservices[🔗 Microservices Architecture]
        S1[Service A] --> DB1[(DB A)]
        S2[Service B] --> DB2[(DB B)]
        S3[Service C] --> DB3[(DB C)]
        S1 <--> S2 <--> S3
        GW[API Gateway] --> S1 & S2 & S3
    end

data.title: Exercise: Identify Boundaries
data.description: For a sample e-commerce application (catalog, cart, checkout, payments, shipping), sketch which capabilities belong together and which should be separate services.
steps: Group related capabilities by change frequency
Propose a service boundary for each group
Justify why each boundary makes sense
data.expectedOutcome: A diagram with 4-6 candidate services and a short rationale for each

items.question: When would you keep a monolith?
items.answer: When the team is small, the domain is simple, or the product is in early validation. Monoliths reduce operational overhead until the domain or team scales.

items.question: What is the biggest cost of microservices?
items.answer: Distributed complexity: network calls, data consistency, observability, and deployment orchestration.

items.question: Does microservices mean more teams?
items.answer: Not necessarily. It enables team autonomy, but requires platform engineering to manage shared infrastructure.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Monolith = one deployable unit; microservices = many independent services
Microservices trade simplicity for scalability and autonomy
Team structure and domain boundaries drive the decision
data.takeaway: Choose the architecture that matches your team size, domain complexity, and scale requirements.
